facility_roles.quote: The Yakutsk array is located in Lena river valley near village Oktyomtsy (50 km South-West of Yakutsk).

intervals.label: array operating
intervals.note: The same paper's abstract says "continuously operating for more than 50 years (since 1970)"; Glushkov et al. (arXiv:0907.0374) say the array "has been observing UHECR events since 1973"; a 2025 Yakutsk paper gives "the entire observation period of 1974-2024". 1973 is used where the body text and the independent paper agree.
intervals.quote: it has been continuously operating since 1973

intervals.label: technical modernization
intervals.note: "...and as a result the array was reduced to its minimal area of 5.62 km2." Whether observations continued during the modernization is not stated.
intervals.quote: During the 2019-2021 period a significant technical modernization was conducted

website.quote: The Yakutsk extensive air shower array studies cosmic rays of extremely high energies above 10 PeV

name: Yakutsk EAS array
notes: No named collaboration is recorded: the array is operated by the Yu.G. Shafer Institute (SHICRA SB RAS) and the papers list institute authors; a note rather than a collaboration record explains this.
The array start is given as 1970, 1973 and 1974 by different Yakutsk-related papers (see the log); 1973 is used.
The facility and the experiment coincide (facility:yakutsk-eas-array).

physics_goals.quote: The Yakutsk extensive air shower array studies cosmic rays of extremely high energies above 10 PeV
physics_goals.value: Study cosmic rays of extremely high energies above 10 PeV: their intensity, energy spectrum, mass composition and origin.

summary.plain: One of the longest-running giant cosmic-ray detectors, in a Siberian river valley. Scintillators, underground muon counters and light detectors have recorded air showers since the 1970s, including three of the highest-energy cosmic rays ever seen.
summary.technical: Yakutsk extensive air shower array near Oktyomtsy (61.70 N, 129.40 E, 100 m): surface scintillators, underground muon detectors and Cherenkov-light PMTs; area up to about 17 km2 (about 1990), now 5.62 km2 after the 2019-2021 modernization; studies cosmic rays above 10 PeV (spectrum, mass composition, muon content, anisotropy).
